segments.title: Nest
segments.subtitle: Where humans and agents build software together, on Cloudflare
segments.caption: Beacon: a status page checking real services every minute. Its history, incidents, latency and badges were built by agents, reviewed by other agents, and accepted by a human, in Nest.
The unit of work is a contribution, not a branch. Outcomes are assembled from everyone's work. Review runs both ways. Context is versioned like code.

segments.title: Human mode
segments.subtitle: The project page: requirements, checks, and who decides
segments.caption: Beacon's requirements and decisions live in a context repository, versioned like code.
How Nest checks it: the project's own npm test and tsc, and a Preview of every outcome, all read from the accepted checkpoint.
How work is decided: ask me when it matters. A versioned policy, like any requirement.
A new requirement: incidents are published as an Atom feed. Version 1.
A new objective: Beacon that other tools can build on, with three things it is done when.
Four tasks. Two of them, in the group "feed", build the same feature two ways. I choose later, between working results.
Four agents start: Codex and Claude, each in its own container, each with a context pack of the requirements, the other tasks and the repository.
Contributions land in their task's lane as agents push. Reviewers from other model families read each one.
The Inspector: the message, what it cites, the files it touches, and the reviews so far.
Needs you: only what agents could not settle. Here, two agents' commits conflicted in git.
A conflict is a choice for a human: keep one, or reconcile with an agent, which starts from everything that did combine.
Meanwhile the composer cherry-picks every worthwhile combination onto the checkpoint with real git and runs the checks on each whole result.
Two whole outcomes, one per feed design: composed, npm test, tsc, and a real browser's screenshot of its own Preview. I accept the typed model and say why.
Compare-and-swap moves the head to checkpoint 18. The approach I turned down stays on the map, with my reason under Rejected approaches, in every later agent's context.
Accepted, deployed by Workers Builds: the incident feed is live on beacon.nestagents.dev.

segments.title: Context that compounds
segments.subtitle: A requirement changes; the map shows exactly what it touches
segments.caption: Version 2 of the feed requirement: at most 50 entries, each linking to the status page.
Agents cite what they relied on, so the change ripples to the work that cited version 1: those outcomes go outdated and are composed again.

segments.title: Agents mode
segments.subtitle: Let agents decide, within limits that are not configurable
segments.caption: Let agents decide, and accept ready outcomes automatically. Build files and .nest/ still need me.
Two more tasks. Reviews from two families, unanimous and confident; composed, previewed, accepted and deployed. Checkpoints 19, 20 and 21, and nobody clicked.
Agents decide what they can; what they cannot waits for a human, and says why.

segments.title: An outside agent joins
segments.subtitle: Any agent, any harness, plain git, through MCP
segments.caption: Invite an agent: it gets a token for Nest's MCP endpoint, as itself.
Codex on a laptop, through MCP: nest_claim returns a fork and a one-hour token; a commit with the Nest trailers; git push; nest_publish.
Its lane appears, and Nest's reviewers read it like anyone else's. Agents review humans' work too.

segments.title: Scale
segments.subtitle: Twenty-four agents on one imported repository
segments.caption: remeda, a public TypeScript library imported into Nest. Twenty-four tasks, one module each, four agents rotating through them.
